title: GitHub - bealesh/neckbeard: Agent plugin that scaffolds tested, cost-honest cloud infrastructure from a versioned module catalog
excerpt: Agent plugin that scaffolds tested, cost-honest cloud infrastructure from a versioned module catalog - bealesh/neckbeard
content_html:
A plugin for your coding agent that turns an app into cloud infrastructure you can actually review, with the monthly bill attached.

Coding agents are great at application code and weirdly confident about infrastructure. Ask one to "deploy this to AWS" and you'll get three hundred lines of plausible HCL, a security group open to the world, an IAM policy with a star in it, and no idea what any of it costs. It reads like the work of someone who has absorbed every blog post and never once been paged. The model isn't lying to you. It has simply never seen the invoice.

neckbeard splits the job. Humans maintain a catalog of OpenTofu modules that are versioned, tested in CI on every change, and scoped to one honest workload shape: a container image, up to ten HTTP, worker, and cron processes, Postgres, object storage, secrets. The agent reads your repo, works out what the app needs, asks you the questions code can't answer, and maps the answers onto catalog inputs. Everything in between is deterministic Go. The planner writes a hash-verified blueprint.yaml, the renderer is a pure function of it, and regeneration refuses to overwrite a file you've touched. The agent never invents infrastructure. If your app needs Redis, you get a named finding that says the catalog doesn't do Redis yet, rather than a module that looks like it might.

It covers AWS, GCP, and Azure, with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, as serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Container Apps) or Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS). The plugin shape is borrowed from ponytail, which proved a plugin can be mostly one good prompt.

Install

Claude Code, as two separate prompts:

/plugin marketplace add bealesh/neckbeard

/plugin install neckbeard@neckbeard

Then open your app's repo and run /neckbeard:analyze. Your first neckbeard command installs the small CLI the plugin drives (a sha256-verified release binary, or go install if you have Go around), and that's the whole setup. Cost estimates and validation lean on tools you may already have, namely Infracost, OpenTofu, and Checkov. /neckbeard:doctor tells you what's missing and what each one buys you.

Codex, Cursor, or anything else that reads a SKILL.md: see INSTALL.md.

What it's like to use

You run /neckbeard:analyze and the agent reads the repo the way a careful new hire would. Dockerfiles, exposed ports, environment variables, health endpoints, the Procfile, the corner of settings.py where Django quietly reads DATABASE_URL. It writes an app profile in which every fact carries a file and line number, every inference carries a confidence, and every assumption is loud. Then it asks you the things it genuinely can't know: how much traffic to expect, how much downtime you'll tolerate, whether that Postgres is one you already run or one you want built, what the worker is for. Your answers get recorded next to the assumptions they resolve, and planning refuses to run while any of them is still open.

/neckbeard:estimate plans against the catalog and shows you the bill before anything exists. /neckbeard:sync scaffolds the infrastructure, the pipelines, and on Kubernetes the cluster manifests, then validates them and tells you precisely what it did and didn't prove. From there you review the files like any other pull request and follow the generated docs/bootstrap.md once per environment, with real credentials in your own hands. The agent never gets those.

Command What it does
/neckbeard:analyze Read the repo into an evidence-backed app-profile.yaml, ask the open questions, propose neckbeard.yaml.
/neckbeard:estimate [comparison] Plan against the catalog and show the monthly cost table, including everything that couldn't be priced. serverless vs kubernetes or solo vs smallteam runs both.
/neckbeard:sync Plan, estimate, scaffold, validate. Your edits are never silently overwritten. Ends with PASSED, FAILED, or NOT EXERCISED for each check.
/neckbeard:doctor [plan|estimate|validate|all] Install the CLI if it's missing and report which tools are present.
/neckbeard:help The short version of this page.

The bill

Nobody tells you what infrastructure costs until the invoice arrives, which is a strange way to make an engineering decision. So neckbeard asks Infracost first. Same reference app (an HTTP service, a worker, a cron job, Postgres), smallest tier, all three environments, live prices:

Cloud Run Container Apps ECS Fargate EKS GKE (regional) AKS
monthly $77 ~$98* $250 $396 $754 ~$801*

The asterisk matters. Infracost can't price Container Apps compute yet, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a low number lie, so the report lists every resource it couldn't price right next to the total. The rest is what you'd want from anyone who has read a cloud bill with their name on it: the idle baseline separated from usage, the usage assumptions written down where you can edit them, low, expected, and high scenarios, and a footer saying where the numbers came from. The table is also how the tool argues. When a solo developer asks for Kubernetes, the numbers say "not yet" so nobody else has to.

What it will and won't claim

Infrastructure tooling has a long tradition of implying more than it has proven. A passing tofu validate has never once meant a thing deploys. neckbeard reports in three levels and insists on showing you the third:

V0   PASSED         tofu validate [prd]
V0   PASSED         checkov policy [prd]        every skip carries a written reason
V0   PASSED         kubeconform (clusters/)
V1   NOT EXERCISED  authenticated plan          requires cloud credentials
V2   NOT EXERCISED  deployment verification     requires cloud credentials

V0 is syntax and policy. Every Checkov skip in the generated config carries a written reason, because a skip without one is a lie about your security posture. V1 is an authenticated plan and V2 is a verified deployment; both need credentials, and both stay NOT EXERCISED until a human runs them. When live runs break, the failures go into the public findings ledger and from there into the catalog. The first real deployment produced ten of them, and five became module fixes the same afternoon. Degraded paths say why: an Azure plus GitLab merge-request plan can't federate, so the generated pipeline says that out loud instead of failing in a way you'd lose an evening to.

What's in the box

Three isolated environments with their own state, sized by tier presets that spell out traffic, availability, recovery objectives, and how many people are actually around to operate the thing. Every preset value is visible and overridable within the catalog's tested envelope, and anything outside that envelope is marked rather than blessed. Pipelines come from one internal model for either CI: test, build, scan (Trivy blocks HIGH and CRITICAL), push, plans on pull requests under a read-only identity, applies on main under a write identity, production gated behind environment protection. There are no static cloud keys anywhere. It's OIDC federation end to end, and a test fails the build if a rendered pipeline so much as mentions AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Networks are private by default, secret managers hold the names the operator fills in (values never pass through neckbeard, its state, or your git history), and managed WAF rules switch on where the tier calls for them.

Where it actually stands

Pre-alpha, and specific about which parts.

Claim Evidence
analyze, plan, estimate, scaffold, validate on all 12 cloud × VCS × runtime paths Static matrix runs in CI on every PR; three unrelated fixture apps onboard end to end
Live deploy, update, and rollback on serverless containers Passed on AWS/GitHub and Azure/GitHub with real database checks (evidence)
Live deploy on GCP, the GitLab lanes, Kubernetes, promotion, recovery drills Not yet. Implemented, NOT EXERCISED

The plugin's product today is the front half: reviewable infrastructure, pipelines, a cost estimate, and a runbook you can hand to whoever holds the credentials. The deployment lifecycle underneath it (neckbeard release, documented in the skill) exists and has worked for real on two lanes, but it stays experimental until it clears the gates in the launch plan. Static validation is not deployment proof. Landing zones, meaning org structure and guardrails, the Path F story in DESIGN.md, are designed and not built.

How it's put together

            you / your agent                      deterministic core
        ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌───────────────────────────┐
repo ──▶│ analyze: facts w/    │  profile   │ plan: catalog @ pinned    │
        │ evidence, questions, ├───────────▶│ versions → blueprint.yaml │
        │ judgment, answers    │  config    │ (hash-verified lockfile)  │
        └──────────────────────┘            └─────────┬─────────────────┘
                                       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                                       ▼              ▼              ▼
                                   estimate       scaffold        validate
                                   Infracost,     ownership       V0 static,
                                   scenarios,     contract:       V1 plan,
                                   unpriced       never silently  V2 deploy,
                                   named          overwrite       each reported

The repository root is the plugin. skills/neckbeard/SKILL.md is the agent's operating manual, commands/ holds the slash commands, and the Go CLI under cmd/ plus the module catalog under catalog/ is the deterministic half. The CLI runs fine without an agent at all:

go install github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/cmd/neckbeard@latest
neckbeard analyze && $EDITOR app-profile.yaml neckbeard.yaml
neckbeard plan && neckbeard estimate && neckbeard scaffold && neckbeard validate

If you've run anything in production for long enough, you know the expensive mistakes rarely live in the application code. They live in the account bill and the 3am page. This is a tool for catching them while they're still a diff.

More, if you want it: DESIGN.md is the full design, kept honest since day one. docs/findings/ is what reality taught us. CONTRIBUTING.md is how to help.

License

Apache-2.0, see LICENSE.

content_html_zh:
A plugin for your coding agent that turns an app into cloud infrastructure you can actually review, with the monthly bill attached.

Coding agents are great at application code and weirdly confident about infrastructure. Ask one to "deploy this to AWS" and you'll get three hundred lines of plausible HCL, a security group open to the world, an IAM policy with a star in it, and no idea what any of it costs. It reads like the work of someone who has absorbed every blog post and never once been paged. The model isn't lying to you. It has simply never seen the invoice.

neckbeard splits the job. Humans maintain a catalog of OpenTofu modules that are versioned, tested in CI on every change, and scoped to one honest workload shape: a container image, up to ten HTTP, worker, and cron processes, Postgres, object storage, secrets. The agent reads your repo, works out what the app needs, asks you the questions code can't answer, and maps the answers onto catalog inputs. Everything in between is deterministic Go. The planner writes a hash-verified blueprint.yaml, the renderer is a pure function of it, and regeneration refuses to overwrite a file you've touched. The agent never invents infrastructure. If your app needs Redis, you get a named finding that says the catalog doesn't do Redis yet, rather than a module that looks like it might.

It covers AWS, GCP, and Azure, with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, as serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Container Apps) or Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS). The plugin shape is borrowed from ponytail, which proved a plugin can be mostly one good prompt.

安装

Claude Code, as two separate prompts:

/plugin marketplace add bealesh/neckbeard

/plugin install neckbeard@neckbeard

Then open your app's repo and run /neckbeard:analyze. Your first neckbeard command installs the small CLI the plugin drives (a sha256-verified release binary, or go install if you have Go around), and that's the whole setup. Cost estimates and validation lean on tools you may already have, namely Infracost, OpenTofu, and Checkov. /neckbeard:doctor tells you what's missing and what each one buys you.

Codex, Cursor, or anything else that reads a SKILL.md: see INSTALL.md.

What it's like to use

You run /neckbeard:analyze and the agent reads the repo the way a careful new hire would. Dockerfiles, exposed ports, environment variables, health endpoints, the Procfile, the corner of settings.py where Django quietly reads DATABASE_URL. It writes an app profile in which every fact carries a file and line number, every inference carries a confidence, and every assumption is loud. Then it asks you the things it genuinely can't know: how much traffic to expect, how much downtime you'll tolerate, whether that Postgres is one you already run or one you want built, what the worker is for. Your answers get recorded next to the assumptions they resolve, and planning refuses to run while any of them is still open.

/neckbeard:estimate plans against the catalog and shows you the bill before anything exists. /neckbeard:sync scaffolds the infrastructure, the pipelines, and on Kubernetes the cluster manifests, then validates them and tells you precisely what it did and didn't prove. From there you review the files like any other pull request and follow the generated docs/bootstrap.md once per environment, with real credentials in your own hands. The agent never gets those.

命令 它的作用
/neckbeard:analyze Read the repo into an evidence-backed app-profile.yaml, ask the open questions, propose neckbeard.yaml.
/neckbeard:estimate [comparison] Plan against the catalog and show the monthly cost table, including everything that couldn't be priced. serverless vs kubernetes or solo vs smallteam runs both.
/neckbeard:sync Plan, estimate, scaffold, validate. Your edits are never silently overwritten. Ends with PASSED, FAILED, or NOT EXERCISED for each check.
/neckbeard:doctor [plan|estimate|validate|all] Install the CLI if it's missing and report which tools are present.
/neckbeard:help The short version of this page.

The bill

Nobody tells you what infrastructure costs until the invoice arrives, which is a strange way to make an engineering decision. So neckbeard asks Infracost first. Same reference app (an HTTP service, a worker, a cron job, Postgres), smallest tier, all three environments, live prices:

Cloud Run Container Apps ECS Fargate EKS GKE (regional) AKS
monthly $77 ~$98* $250 $396 $754 ~$801*

The asterisk matters. Infracost can't price Container Apps compute yet, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a low number lie, so the report lists every resource it couldn't price right next to the total. The rest is what you'd want from anyone who has read a cloud bill with their name on it: the idle baseline separated from usage, the usage assumptions written down where you can edit them, low, expected, and high scenarios, and a footer saying where the numbers came from. The table is also how the tool argues. When a solo developer asks for Kubernetes, the numbers say "not yet" so nobody else has to.

What it will and won't claim

Infrastructure tooling has a long tradition of implying more than it has proven. A passing tofu validate has never once meant a thing deploys. neckbeard reports in three levels and insists on showing you the third:

V0   PASSED         tofu validate [prd]
V0   PASSED         checkov policy [prd]        every skip carries a written reason
V0   PASSED         kubeconform (clusters/)
V1   NOT EXERCISED  authenticated plan          requires cloud credentials
V2   NOT EXERCISED  deployment verification     requires cloud credentials

V0 is syntax and policy. Every Checkov skip in the generated config carries a written reason, because a skip without one is a lie about your security posture. V1 is an authenticated plan and V2 is a verified deployment; both need credentials, and both stay NOT EXERCISED until a human runs them. When live runs break, the failures go into the public findings ledger and from there into the catalog. The first real deployment produced ten of them, and five became module fixes the same afternoon. Degraded paths say why: an Azure plus GitLab merge-request plan can't federate, so the generated pipeline says that out loud instead of failing in a way you'd lose an evening to.

What's in the box

Three isolated environments with their own state, sized by tier presets that spell out traffic, availability, recovery objectives, and how many people are actually around to operate the thing. Every preset value is visible and overridable within the catalog's tested envelope, and anything outside that envelope is marked rather than blessed. Pipelines come from one internal model for either CI: test, build, scan (Trivy blocks HIGH and CRITICAL), push, plans on pull requests under a read-only identity, applies on main under a write identity, production gated behind environment protection. There are no static cloud keys anywhere. It's OIDC federation end to end, and a test fails the build if a rendered pipeline so much as mentions AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Networks are private by default, secret managers hold the names the operator fills in (values never pass through neckbeard, its state, or your git history), and managed WAF rules switch on where the tier calls for them.

它的实际位置

Claim 证据
analyze, plan, estimate, scaffold, validate on all 12 cloud × VCS × runtime paths Static matrix runs in CI on every PR; three unrelated fixture apps onboard end to end
Live deploy, update, and rollback on serverless containers Passed on AWS/GitHub and Azure/GitHub with real database checks (evidence)
Live deploy on GCP, the GitLab lanes, Kubernetes, promotion, recovery drills 还没有。 Implemented, NOT EXERCISED

The plugin's product today is the front half: reviewable infrastructure, pipelines, a cost estimate, and a runbook you can hand to whoever holds the credentials. The deployment lifecycle underneath it (neckbeard release, documented in the skill) exists and has worked for real on two lanes, but it stays experimental until it clears the gates in the launch plan. Static validation is not deployment proof. Landing zones, meaning org structure and guardrails, the Path F story in DESIGN.md, are designed and not built.

How it's put together

            you / your agent                      deterministic core
        ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌───────────────────────────┐
repo ──▶│ analyze: facts w/    │  profile   │ plan: catalog @ pinned    │
        │ evidence, questions, ├───────────▶│ versions → blueprint.yaml │
        │ judgment, answers    │  config    │ (hash-verified lockfile)  │
        └──────────────────────┘            └─────────┬─────────────────┘
                                       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                                       ▼              ▼              ▼
                                   estimate       scaffold        validate
                                   Infracost,     ownership       V0 static,
                                   scenarios,     contract:       V1 plan,
                                   unpriced       never silently  V2 deploy,
                                   named          overwrite       each reported

The repository root is the plugin. skills/neckbeard/SKILL.md is the agent's operating manual, commands/ holds the slash commands, and the Go CLI under cmd/ plus the module catalog under catalog/ is the deterministic half. The CLI runs fine without an agent at all:

go install github.com/bealesh/neckbeard/cmd/neckbeard@latest
neckbeard analyze && $EDITOR app-profile.yaml neckbeard.yaml
neckbeard plan && neckbeard estimate && neckbeard scaffold && neckbeard validate

If you've run anything in production for long enough, you know the expensive mistakes rarely live in the application code. They live in the account bill and the 3am page. This is a tool for catching them while they're still a diff.

More, if you want it: DESIGN.md is the full design, kept honest since day one. docs/findings/ is what reality taught us. CONTRIBUTING.md is how to help.
